idiom_name: private static holder class with a static final field
implementation_notes: The JDK has no Lazy<T>, so the idiomatic replacement for the classic null-marker test is the initialization-on-demand holder: the initialiser runs when the holder class is first referenced, and JLS 12.4.2 guarantees the class-initialisation step is performed once and atomically, so every reader sees a fully built value with no synchronisation on the fast path. It replaces the null check entirely for static state and is the canonical 'lazy singleton' in Java. Limitation: it only works for static state - instance fields still need the volatile-DCL or AtomicReference form.
pitfalls: Class initialisation is a one-shot: if the initialiser fails, the JVM marks the class erroneous and every later access throws ExceptionInInitializerError/NoClassDefFoundError - there is no retry and no reset, so the initialiser must not depend on transient resources.
It cannot be used for per-instance laziness (each instance would need its own holder, defeating the idiom), and reaching any of the holder's members triggers the build.

Circular class initialisation between two threads deadlocks (a single thread may re-enter initialisation, two threads may not cross it), so initialisers must not call back into unrelated lazy holders.
Reflection/DI frameworks that touch the holder class early (or serialise it) can initialise the value during startup, silently undoing the laziness.

variants.name: Volatile double-checked locking (instance state)
variants.idiom_name: volatile field with a synchronised slow path (or AtomicReference CAS)
variants.implementation_notes: For instance fields, values that must be reassignable, or holders that need a reset, the pattern is double-checked locking over a volatile field: the fast path reads the volatile field, the slow path synchronises, re-tests and publishes. From Java 5 onward the JMM's volatile semantics make this correct (write-then-volatile-write, volatile-read-then-read behaviour), which is exactly why the identical code was broken before Java 5; AtomicReference.compareAndSet is the equivalent lock-free formulation. This variant replaces the holder class only where the holder cannot be used - it is more code and more failure modes.
pitfalls: Removing volatile (or forgetting it on a field that was volatile in a previous revision) reintroduces the broken pre-Java-5 pattern: another thread can see a non-null reference to a partially constructed object.

The local copy of the field is load-bearing: re-reading the field on the fast path can return null after another thread published, and the classic 'return index' instead of 'return i' variants re-read it.
The secondary test inside the lock is mandatory; without it the slow path rebuilds the value that the first waiter already produced (double side effects: two connections, two registrations).

Volatile reads are cheap but not free, and publishing a mutable object through a volatile field only publishes that field - the object's own state must be safely published too (final fields, or build in the constructor and never mutate).
